passages.happening:
The Philistines fight Israel, and the men of Israel flee. Many fall dead on Mount Gilboa (verse 1). The Philistines press hard after Saul and his sons, and they kill Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua (verse 2).

The battle turns against Saul. The archers find him, and he is badly wounded (verse 3). He tells his armor-bearer to kill him, ‘or these uncircumcised men will come and run me through and torture me’ (verse 4). The armor-bearer is terrified and will not do it, and Saul takes his own life (verse 4). When the armor-bearer sees that Saul is dead, he dies with him (verse 5).

“So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that same day” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Here the book ends, and with it the reign of Israel's first king. What Samuel foretold at Endor comes true the next day. The king the people asked for, so that he could go out before them and fight their battles, dies in battle against the very enemy he was meant to defeat.

The battle took place around the end of the eleventh century BC, usually dated about 1010 BC, though the dates of Saul's reign are uncertain. Mount Gilboa is a ridge on the southeastern side of the Jezreel Valley.

Saul's fear of being taken alive was well founded. Ancient armies often tortured and humiliated captured kings, and the Philistines had already blinded and mocked Samson.

Jonathan, who loved David and never grasped for the throne, dies beside his father. The chapter does not explain why the faithful son shares the unfaithful father's end. Scripture is honest that in a broken world the innocent often suffer in the ruin others cause.

The chapter is told with great restraint. The narrator does not gloat or preach, and does not even mention God. The phrase ‘died together that same day’ gathers father, sons, servant and soldiers into one end.
passages.later:
Chronicles tells the same end: ‘So Saul died together with his three sons and all his house’ (1 Chronicles 10:6).

David's lament in the next book begins, “Your glory, O Israel, lies slain on your heights. How the mighty have fallen!” (2 Samuel 1:19).
passages.hard:
Saul took his own life. How does the Bible treat this, and what should be said about it?

The Bible records a few such deaths, among them Abimelech in Judges, Saul and his armor-bearer here, Ahithophel in 2 Samuel, Zimri in 1 Kings, and Judas in Matthew. In each case it reports the act without long comment. It never presents taking one's own life as a good or honorable way out.

Here the narrator shows a man in agony, wounded, cut off from God and afraid of torture, and treats him with sorrow, not contempt. The men of Jabesh bury him with honor, and David will lament him.

Christian traditions have differed on the spiritual state of those who take their own lives. Many have taught that it is a grave sin against God's gift of life, while insisting that salvation rests on Christ's grace and not on the manner of a person's death, and that despair and anguish of mind must be met with compassion. The chapter is not a pattern to follow. It is a tragedy to grieve.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: At the end Saul could get no answer from God, after years of refusing to listen, and Jonathan died faithful beside him. Ask what the difference between them was, and what it was not. And if this chapter weighs on you because of a loss of your own, ask who you could tell today.

passages.happening:
When the Israelites in the valley and across the Jordan see that the army has fled and that Saul and his sons are dead, they abandon their towns and flee, and the Philistines move in (verse 7).

The next day the Philistines come to strip the dead and find Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa (verse 8). They cut off Saul's head, strip off his armor, and send word through their land, to the temples of their idols and to their people (verse 9). They put his armor in the temple of the Ashtoreths ‘and hung his body on the wall of Beth-shan’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
By winning at Gilboa the Philistines cut the country in two. The Israelites in the valley, and even across the Jordan, left their towns. Philistine power reached its height in these years. It was David who would later break it.

Beth-shan was a fortified city where the Jezreel Valley meets the Jordan Valley, guarding a key crossing. It had been an Egyptian garrison town in earlier centuries.

Stripping a defeated king, putting his armor in a temple and showing his body in public were ways of saying that the victors' gods had won. The Ashtoreths were forms of Astarte, a goddess of love and war widely worshiped in Canaan and Phoenicia.

The chapter tells all this plainly and briefly, and it does not linger.

The word fall runs through the chapter. Israel's men fell slain, Saul and his armor-bearer fell, and Saul and his sons are found fallen. David's lament will take up the same word.
passages.later:
Chronicles adds what the Philistines did with his head: ‘They put his armor in the temple of their gods and hung his head in the temple of Dagon’ (1 Chronicles 10:10).

The Philistines had shamed another of Israel's champions the same way: ‘Then the Philistines seized him, gouged out his eyes, and brought him down to Gaza’ (Judges 16:21).
passages.asks: The Philistines made Saul's death a public show. Ask how you speak of the failures of people who have fallen, whether with mockery or with grief. And ask what it says about a people when they treat a defeated enemy with contempt.

passages.happening:
“When the people of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, all their men of valor set out, journeyed all night, and retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan” (verses 11-12). At Jabesh they burn the bodies.

“Then they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and they fasted seven days” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Jabesh-gilead lay across the Jordan to the east, about a night's march away. Saul's first great act as king had been to save it from the Ammonites. Now its men repay that debt at great risk to themselves.

To leave a body unburied was among the worst dishonors of the ancient world, and to give it burial was a sacred duty. Burning the bodies before burying the bones was unusual in Israel, where it was not the normal practice. Many suggest it was because of what had been done to the bodies.

They bury the bones under a tamarisk tree, a hardy tree of dry country. Saul had held court under a tamarisk at Gibeah. A seven-day fast was the usual mourning for the dead, the grief and honor given to a king.

The book that began with a childless woman's prayer at Shiloh ends with a fast at a graveside. The last act of 1 Samuel is an act of loyalty.
passages.later:
When David became king, he thanked the men of Jabesh for this kindness, and later he moved the bones of Saul and Jonathan to the family grave: ‘And they buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in Zela in the land of Benjamin, in the tomb of Saul’s father Kish’ (2 Samuel 21:14).

Joseph mourned his father for the same seven days: ‘Joseph mourned for his father seven days’ (Genesis 50:10).
passages.asks: The men of Jabesh remembered what Saul had done for them, and walked all night to honor him. Ask whose kindness to you you have never repaid. And ask whether you can honor someone's good deeds even when their life ended badly.
